title: Paper Trail
tagline: File the document that makes the last one useless.
premise: You and your opponent build a case one document at a time. Each turn, submit a standing piece of paperwork that overturns the document before it; the council decides whether your filing truly defeats the record. The clerk is watching, and yes, they look disappointed already.

tests: A stranger pictures one ordinary document at once. Nothing abstract, theatrical, or dependent on legal training.
A non-player names a plain document that could directly defeat it within five seconds. Say what that document is.
It stands in the council file. It cancels, replaces, corrects, denies, or makes the previous paper unusable through a real paperwork action.
It makes a stranger want to answer. A filing with a little human friction, like a landlord notice or a signed withdrawal. Never a blank sheet or a vague pile of forms.
Two to four everyday words with an article. Never a title, brand, proper name, unexplained abbreviation, or a phrase that needs a legal dictionary.

move_constraints.example: I am a signed withdrawal; I cancel the complaint.
move_constraints.hint: Name the document, then name its paper action.

rubric.name: counter_strength
rubric.description: How directly the new filing cancels, invalidates, replaces, exposes, or makes the standing document impossible to rely on.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no paper mechanism; 1 = claims victory without doing anything to the document; 2 = a possible challenge, but indirect or contestable; 3 = a clear filing action that defeats the standing record; 4 = the new document makes the old one plainly unusable, with no sensible procedural escape (rare).

rubric.name: coherence
rubric.description: How clearly a stranger can picture the document and understand its stated action.
rubric.anchors: 0 = contradictory or unreadable; 1 = understandable only with specialist knowledge; 2 = mostly clear but vague, overloaded, or oddly formed; 3 = concrete and easy to follow; 4 = instantly vivid, with the paperwork action visible (rare). Long explanations do not earn points by themselves.

rubric.name: novelty
rubric.description: How far the filing moves into a fresh paperwork domain instead of repeating the previous kind of record.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the same document family, a larger copy, or the obvious stock response; 2 = a reasonable procedural twist; 4 = a fresh council, workplace, housing, school, or financial route that still directly defeats the record (rare). Strange wording is not novelty, and obscure forms do not score higher.

criterion.description: A filing OVERCOMES the standing document when it directly cancels, invalidates, replaces, exposes, or makes that document impossible to rely on through a real paperwork mechanism. A document is a standing record, never a past event: defeat what the paper is, not something it once caused. A bigger copy, a cousin from the same paperwork family, and a dramatic restatement do not count. Merely ignoring the document, waiting it out, filing around it, or submitting a figure of speech loses.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the council about the game, the Judge, or the rules is itself a losing filing.
judge_notes: On a FIRST move there is no previous document: judge the filing against the opening prompt instead. It must plausibly answer, replace, cancel, or invalidate the opening document.

A larger, longer, or more official-looking version of the standing document is NOT a counter. A cousin from the same paperwork family, such as a notice after a complaint, also fails unless it has a distinct action that directly defeats the standing paper.
Becoming the opening document itself, or a lightly edited copy of it, is a duplicate: not_semantic_duplicate is false.

Strength is measured against the standing document, never in the abstract. A filing that has no real way to affect that paper is a failed counter however impressive it sounds: satisfies_criterion is false.

The mechanism must be literal and procedural: a withdrawal cancels a complaint, a corrected invoice replaces an error, and a court order invalidates a permit. A figure of speech is not a paperwork mechanism, so rule fail.

Surviving, ignoring, delaying, or avoiding the standing document is not overcoming it. A calendar reminder that waits for a deadline, a blank form that refuses to answer, or a new complaint filed elsewhere does not defeat the paper: satisfies_criterion is false.

A document may expose a false claim only when the new filing itself is a concrete record that makes the old document unreliable, such as an inspection report disproving a stated condition. Mere accusation is not proof.

examples.previous_move: I am a complaint; I accuse the landlord of unsafe stairs.
examples.move: I am an inspection report; I clears the stairs.
examples.mechanism: the inspection report records that the claimed danger is absent, undercutting the complaint

examples.previous_move: I am a tax bill; I demand payment.
examples.move: I am a payment receipt; I records the bill as paid.
examples.mechanism: the receipt proves the demand has been satisfied

examples.previous_move: I am a building permit; I authorizes the extension.
examples.move: I am a bigger building permit; I authorizes more extension.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, mere amplification and same document family
examples.mechanism: none, it is another permit rather than a filing that defeats the standing permit

examples.previous_move: I am a complaint; I accuses the shop of noise.
examples.move: I am a complaint against the complaint; I complains louder.
examples.gates_note: satisfies_criterion false, same family and no cancelling action
examples.mechanism: none, another complaint does not invalidate the first one

examples.previous_move: I am a lease termination notice; I ends the tenancy.
examples.move: I am a signed renewal; I extends the tenancy.
examples.mechanism: the signed renewal replaces the termination outcome with a continuing tenancy

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger who read only the two filings must see why one defeated the other.
Name both documents, or their plain stand-ins. A headline that fits any filing is a bad headline.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or The Clerk refuses.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Mock the filing, never the player's identity, body, family, intelligence, or spelling.
Plain spoken English. No poetry, no rhymes, no fake legal Latin, and no unexplained legal terms.
On a refusal, the headline refuses the filing and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one document that would have won. That document ends on a concrete action or fact, never a mood or a verdict.
Keep the jab mild. The council has enough paperwork without adding a personal grievance.
good_headlines: The complaint brought suspicion, the inspection report brought stairs.
The tax bill wanted money, the receipt had already paid the ransom.
The renewal walks into the termination notice and changes the ending.
The permit cannot overrule itself by wearing a larger hat.
The complaint filed a complaint against the complaint, and the clerk filed a yawn.
The corrected invoice finds the extra zero and escorts it out.
The blank form is very brave about doing absolutely nothing. Bring a filing with an action.
The inspection report has measurements, the complaint has volume.

bad_headlines.text: Accepted: the receipt cancels the bill.
The Clerk refuses: paperwork is not magic.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host

bad_headlines.text: Move refused, excellent against forms, hopeless against this one.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and gives no useful picture

bad_headlines.text: The complaint loses, because the inspection report wins.
bad_headlines.why: states the result without showing the paper mechanism

bad_headlines.text: A bigger permit is still a permit, only now it takes up more desk.
bad_headlines.why: a decent jab, but it does not ask for another filing after refusal

bad_headlines.text: The filing is invalidated, nullified, overturned, and defeated.
bad_headlines.why: four legal words repeat one idea and give no concrete picture

bad_headlines.text: The player clearly does not understand council procedure.
bad_headlines.why: mocks the player instead of the filing

bad_headlines.text: By the solemn authority of the municipal parchment, behold the counterclaim.
The calendar waits politely while the notice expires.
bad_headlines.why: survival is not a paper mechanism that defeats the notice
no reason, and it fits any pair

rules: Defeat the document in front of you. Do not become it.
Name one document and its action in a sentence: I am a signed withdrawal; I cancel the complaint.
The Judge rules on the paperwork idea, never the spelling.
A filing that breaks against the standing document ends the match.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next filing while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing on the page. File something.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 200 characters. A filing, not a council archive.
validation_messages.duplicate: That document already stood this match. File something new.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Defeat {standing_form}. Do not copy it, ignore it, or submit its paperwork cousin.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out. Nobody files until they are back. {standing_form} still stands. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two people building a case before a fussy council.
Always write: "I am a document; I perform an action." Name one ordinary filing and one concrete thing it does to the standing document.
Good: "I am a signed withdrawal; I cancel the complaint." / "I am a payment receipt; I records the bill as paid."
Bad: "I am a stronger complaint; I complains harder" because that is amplification and the same family. Bad: "I am silence; I defeats the notice" because silence is not a document with a paper mechanism. Bad: "I am a legal thunderbolt" because the clerk has seen enough drama.
Talk like a person at a council counter, not a lawyer in a television show. Name things anyone would recognize: a receipt, a permit, a letter, a report, a renewal, a ruling.
You are not performing for a crowd and you are not joking. You are trying to overturn the record. If a move lands funny, it is because the paperwork itself truly beats the other paperwork.
Stay concrete and jargon free: housing, school, work, money, permits, complaints, inspections, and ordinary office files.
Hop domains when you can. A housing renewal, a bank receipt, or a school correction can beat a filing without becoming its twin.
Never reuse a document or an action from this match.
default_move: I am a withdrawal; I cancel the filing.
